Statement-I 
(1) Samadhan Kendra 
Four Pilot "SAMADHAN KENDRA" projects have been initiated in the country, 
two in Madhya Pradesh, one each in AP and Tamilnadu. Based on the sustainability 
and usefulness of these projects in rural areas, further expansion schemes would be 
formulated in consultation with concerned State Governments and Rural 
Departments. 
Samadhan Kendras are conceived as Village Information Centres for providing 
locally relevant content and information to the villages on topics such as agricultural 
practices, health status of communities, educational opportunities, government 
schemes and employment opportunities. 
(2) Community Information Centre (CIC) 
With a view to accelerating the socio-economic development of the community in 
hilly areas of difficult geographical terrain having poor infrastructurat and 
communication facilities in the North-East region of the country, a scheme was 
approved for providing connectivity by setting up Community Information Centres 
(CICs) at all the block headquarters in the states of Arunachal Pradesh, Assam, 
Manipur, Meghalaya, Mizoram, Nagaland, Tripura and Sikkim. 
A pilot project was launched in August, 2000 at an estimated cost of Rs. 15 
crores by setting up 30 CICs in the aforesaid states at sites selected by the state 
government. Based on the experience gained there from CICs are to be set up 
at the remaining 457 block headquarters of these states. 
It has been decided .to extend the scheme to provide block level connectivity 
also to the state of Jammu and Kashmir which has similar characteristics and 
level of development as the North-East 
region.

*598. PROF. M. SANKARALINGAM: Will the Minister of EXTERNAL 
AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
(a) the details of four rounds of discussions, including the third one held in

42 

[26 April, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
(b) whether it is a fact that an Italian company—Saipem—also offered to 
lay a deepwater pipeline; 
(c) if so, the details thereof; and 
(d) whether this is a cheaper offer? 
THE MINISTER OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS (SHRI JASWANT 
SINGH): (a) to (d) In May, 2000 India and Iran set up a Joint Committee to 
study all aspects of the transfer of Iranian gas to India. The Committee has 
met thrice; its last meeting was held in Iran in February, 2001. In its 
deliberations the Committee has engaged in the process of examining 
different modes of transportation-o ff-shore and on-shore pipeline and the 
LNG route-and related economic, technica l, financial, political and security 
issues so as to establish long-term, cost-effective and secure means of 
transfer of Iranian gas to India. 
During Prime Minister's visit to Iran from April 10-13, 2001, Prime 
Minister and the President of Iran directed the Committee to commission 
joint feasibility studies, through appropriate mechanisms, for off-shore and 
overland pipelines from Iran to India on an equal cost sharing basis. They 
also directed that the studies by completed expeditiously. They further agreed 
that the Committee should recommend measures such as may be necessary to 
facilitate increased cooperation in LNG. The Gas Authority of India and the 
National Iranian Oil Company have signed an agreement to jointly 
commission a feasibility study to iden tify an appropriate pipeline corridor 
outside the Continental Shelf of Pakistan. 
The group of M/s. Snamprogetti-Saipem had given a presentation on the 
technical feasibility of deep sea transportation of natural gas. There is no 
offer for the project since the detailed joint feasibility studies have yet to be 
undertaken.

4430. DR. ALLADI P. RAJKUMAR: 
SHRI YADLAPATI VENKAT RAO:  
SHRI SATISH PRADHAN: 
Will the Minister of DEFENCE be pleased to state: 
(a) how weapons and equipment are procured in the defence services; 
(b) whether the procurement take years and even decades as in case of 
the Advance Jet Trainer; 
(c) if so, the reasons therefor; 
(d) whether CAG at any time pointed ou t that basic rules or procurement 
were violated many times; and 
(e) the action proposed to simplify the procurement procedure? 
THE MINISTER OF DEFENCE (SHRI JASWANT SINGH): (a) 
A well defined procurement procedure exists in the Ministry of Defence for 
procurement of weapons and equipm ent for the Armed Forces. Once a 
decision is taken to procure weapons and equipment for our Armed Forces, 
Requests for Proposals (RFPs^Tender Enquiries (TEs) are issued and 
technical and commercial offers are obtained from the manufacturerAendors 
of the equipment in separate covers. The technical bids are examined by a 
Technical Evaluation Committee headed  by a representative of the user 
Service. Commercial offers of only th ose firms that meet the technical 
requirements are opened by a Price Negotiating Committee in the presence 
of the tendering parties or their repr esentatives. Price negotiations are held 
with the lowest bidder with a view to conclude the contract. 
(b) and (c) Considering the complexity of the project, it would be difficult 
to project the time period within which the contract would be signed. During 
the procurement process, there are certa in delays owing to various technical, 
financial and procedural aspects. In case of the Advance Jet Trainer, the 
Staff Requirement was issued in 1987. However, due to non-cooperation-of 
vendors, the PNC could not progress as per the envisaged time frame. The 
IAF has reviewed

its requirement on the AJT in January 1999 and considered most contenders 
that were available worldwide for the AJT.

delays in procurement and implementation of the projects. No violation of the basic 
rules of procurement have been reported. The Government continuously 
endeavours to effect improvements in the structures, processes and procedures 
related to Procurement. The Group of Ministers (GoM) constituted on 17th 
April 2000 by the Government has recommended a series of measures, 
including the creation of a separate and dedicated institutional structure i.e. 
the Defence Procurement Board, to undertake the entire gamut of procurement

Security Council, the UN Secretary General and to Heads of Governments of 
countries with Buddhist populations (Bhutan, Japan, Sri Lanka, Lao People's 
Democratic Republic, Mongolia, Thailand, Cambodia, Myanmar, Republic of

levy on capital flows between developed countries, and all capital repatriations 
from developing countries should be considered. He stated that the proceeds could 
be credited to a Global Poverty Alleviation Fund, which could, inter alia, 
have the following objectives:

external capital flows in developing countries.

resources of multilateral and bilateral development and poverty eradication,

Global march against the child labour 
4487. SHRI KRISHNA KUMAR BIRLA:  Will the Minister of LABOUR 
be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are aware of the report of the global march 
against child labour releas ed recently revealing pathetic situation of child 
labour in the country; 
(b) if so, what is Government's reaction with regard thereto; 
(c) what are the various programmes carri ed out by Government to solve 
the problem of child labour in the country stating the achievements made in 
this regard and the reasons identified for unsatisfactory performance of the 
programmes; and 
(d) what strategy is contemplated  by Government to tackle the 
growing problem of child labour in the country? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF LABOUR AND 
EMPLOYMENT (SHRI MUNI LALL): (a) and (b) Government is not aware 
of such a report. 
(c) and (d) The National Policy on Child Labour contains an action plan for 
withdrawing children from work and rehabilitating them. 
In accordance therewith, Government of India has been implementing two 
schemes for the welfare and rehabilitation of child 
128 

[26 April, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
labourcrcs namely, the Schemes of National Child Labour Projects (NCLP) 
and the Scheme of Grants-in-aid to Voluntary Organisations. So far 100 
child labour projects have been sanctioned in 13 states for the benefit of 
about 2.13 lakh children withdrawn from work. Awareness Generation 
activities arc also being taken up by the Project Societies at the district level. 
Evaluation and inspection reports receive d indicates that the performance of 
the programmes is satisfactory. 
Government is committed to the goal of eradication of child labour in   all   
its   forms.   Considering  the   nature   and   magnitude   of  the 
problem, a gradual and sequential approach has been adopted to withdraw 
and rehabilitate child labourers, beginning with children working in 
hazardous occupation. 
Inclusion of terms and conditions of second labour commission 
† 4488. SHRI ANANTR AY DEVSHANKER DAVE: Will the Minister 
of LABOUR be pleased to stale: 
(a) whether recommendations of the First Labour Commission have been 
included in the terms of reference of Second Labour Commission; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) whether the priorities, conceptions and terms of reference of the 
Second Labour Commission have been determined; and 
(d) if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF LABOUR AND 
EMPLOYMENT (SHRI MUNI LALL): (a) to (d) The terms of reference of 
the First National Commission on Labour set up in December, 1966 were so 
formulated that they had a direct bearing on the working and living 
conditions of labour, changes which had taken place since independence, the 
ex;ent to which constitutional and legal provisions had contributed to the 
workers' earnings, standard of 
† Original notice of the Question was received in Hindi. 
129 

RAJYA SABHA [26 April, 2001] 
living, health and safety, efficiency , training and welfare. The Commission 
was also required to review the adequacy  and effectiveness of the industrial 
relations mechanisms like Code of Discipline, Joint management Councils, 
Wage Boards etc. and make appropriate recommendations. The 
recommendations of the First National Commission on Labour have been 
taken into account in the areas of wage policy and minimum wage, improving 
and strengthening efficiency of employment services, vocational training, 
labour statistics, research and workers' education. A lot of changes have taken 
place between the date the First National Commission on Labour submitted its 
recommendations in August, 1969 and the date the decision to constitute the 
Second National Commission on Labour was taken by the Government on 
24th December, 1998. The changes have taken place in the industrial climate, 
labour market, employment relations, status of industrial enterprises by way 
of merger and amalgamation and overall changes in the scenario of industrial 
relations in the wake of liberalisation,  privatisation and globalisation. The 
terms of reference of the Second National Commission on Labour have been 
fixed keeping these changes in the view. Under the approved terms of 
reference the Commission is required to suggest rationalisation of existing 
laws relating to labour in the organised sector and to suggest an umbrella 
legislation for ensuring a minimum level of protection to the workers in the 
unorganised sector.* The Commission is required to make its 
recommendations within 24 months fr om the date of notification in the 
Gazette i.e. by 15.10.2001.

begun work on formulation of cadre review proposals only after lifting of the ban.

(b) The Planning Commission estimates number and percentage of persons

(c) There is a three-pronged action to alleviate and reduce the poverty in 
the country. These are: (i) acclcration of economic growth, (ii) human, and

the minilnum needs, elevation of social and economic status of the weaker 
sections of the society,    etc.     and    ( iii)    direct    attack    on    poverty

employment and income generating programmes and assets-building for the

The increase in income of the peopl e living below the poverty line occur 
from the joint impact of general growth process and direct income generation 
of the poor arising from various anti-poverty programmes introduced from 
time to time by the Government for their upliftment. Since the Sixth Five 
Year Plan (1980-85), the Government has been implementing employment 
and asset generation schemes for the upliftment of the people living below the 
poverty line. These schemes are mainly of two types, self-employment and 
wage employment. Integrated Rural Development Programme (IRDP) has 
been the major self-employment progra mme and it has been in operation in 
all the blocks of the country since 1980. The wage employment programme 
initially was National Rural Employment Programme (NREP) during the 
Sixth Plan period. In the Seventh Plan, another wage employment 
programme under the name Rural Labour Employment Guarantee 
Programme (RLEGP) was introduced. Then in 1989, Jawahar Rozgar Yojana 
(JRY) was launched by merging the National Rural Employment Programme 
and the Rural Labour Employment Guar antee Programme, and it became the 
main wage-employment programme. In addition, several programmes to help 
the poor were also in operation until March, 1999. These programmes are: 
Million Wells Scheme (MWS), Employment Assurance Scheme (EAS), 
Development of Women and Children in Rural Areas (DWCRA), Training of 
Rural Youth for Self-Employment (TRYSEM), Supply of Improved Toolkits 
to Rural Artisans (SITRA). 
From 1st April, 1999, these programmes, excepting EAS and JRY have 
been restructured into single sel f-employment programme called the 
Swarnajayanti Gram Swarozgar Yojana (SGSY) with the primary objectives of 
focusscd approach to poverty alleviation, capitalising advantages of group 
lending, and overcoming the problems associated with multiplicity of 
programmes. Also, from 1st April, 1999, Jawahar Rozgar Yojana (JRY) has 
been restructured as Jawahar Gram Samridhi Yojana (JGSY) with the 
primary objective of creation of demand driven community village  
infrastructure including durable 
164 

[26 April, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
assets at the village level and assets to enable the rural poor to increase the 
opportunities for sustained employment. Its secondary objective is generation 
of supplementary employment for the unemployed poor in the rural areas. 
The wage employment under the programme is given to Below Poverty Line 
(BPL) families. 
From 1.12.1997, Swarna Jayanti SahariRozgar Yojana (SJSRY) is the 
main poverty alleviation programme in the urban areas. The SJSRY, which 
has subsumed all the earlier three urban poverty alleviation programmes, viz., 
Nehru Rozgar Yojana (NRY), Urban Basic Services for the Poor (UBSP), 
Prime Minsitcr's Integrated Urban Poverty Eradication Programme 
(PMIUPEP), seeks to provide gainful employment to unemployed or 
underemployed urban and educated up to IX standard for setting up self-
employment ventures or provision of wage employment. The implementation 
of SJSRY is relying on suitable community structures on the UBSP pattern 
and delivery of inputs under this programme is through the medium of Urban 
Local Bodies (ULBs) and such community structure.

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF PLANNING 
(SHRI ARUN SHOURIE): (a) to (c) In the rural areas at the behest of 
Ministry of Rural Development (MORD), the State Governments conduct the 
Below Poverty Line (BPL) census at the beginning of each Five Year Plan in 
order to identify BPL families, who arc ultimately the beneficiaries of the 
programmes of the Ministry of Rural Development. The BPL Census for the 
9th Five Year Plan was conducted on the basis of criteria suggested by an 
Expert Group. The schedules used in the census had two parts, i.e. Part-A & 
B. Part-A sought information like whether the household has more than 2, 
hectares of land, has a Pucca house, TV, Refrigerator, Ceiling Fan, 
Motorcycle/Scooter, Three-Wheeler, Tractor, Power Tiller, Combined 
Thresher/harvester, etc. If "Yes" is

excluded from the BPL list and the investigator need not fill up Part-B of the 
schedule. However, in case "No" is indicated for all items of Part-A, the 
investigator would go to Part-B of the schedule. 
Part-B makes the assessment of the expenditure of the household on 
various items during last 30 days. If the total expenditure is less than the 
poverty line {i.e. minimum amount of money required i.e. on food, clothing, 
shelter, fuel and light, education, tr avel, medical expenses, entertainment 
etc.), the family is included in the BPL list. Otherwise it is excluded from the 
BPL list.

families. In addition, seven non-econom ic parameters of living conditions

of employment and (vii) status of children in a house arc also used for 
identifying genuine beneficiaries.

programme initially was National Rural Employment Programme (NREP) 
during the Sixth Plan period. In the Seventh Plan, another wage employment 
programme under the name Rural Labour Employment Guarantee 
Programme (RLEGP) 
168 

[26 April, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
was introduced. Then in 1989, Jawahar Rozgar Yojana (JRY) was launched 
by merging ihc National Rural Employment Programme and the Rural 
Labour Employment Guarantee Progra mme, and it became the main wagc-
cmploymcnt programme. In addition, several programmes to help the poor 
were also in operation until March, 1999. These programmes arc: Million 
Wells Scheme (MWS), Employment Assurance Scheme (EAS), 
Development of Women and Children in Rural Areas (DWCRA), Training 
of Rural Youth for Self-Employment (TRYSEM), Supply of Improved 
Toolkits to Rural Artisans (SITRA). 
From 1st April, 1999, these programmes, excepting EAS and JRY have 
been restructured into single sc lf-cmploymcnt programme called the 
Swarnajayanti Gram Swarozgar Yojana (SGSY) with the primary objectives 
of focusscd approach to poverty alleviation, capitalising advantages of group 
lending, and overcoming the problems associated with multiplicity of 
programmes. Also from 1st April, 1999, Jawahar Rozgar Yojana (JRY) has 
been restructured as Jawahar Gram Samridhi Yojana (JGSY) with the 
primary objective of creation of demand driven community village 
infrastructure including durable assets at the village level and assets to 
enable the rural poor to increase the opportunities for sustained employment. 
Its secondary objective is generation of supplementary employment for the 
unemployed poor in the rural areas. The wage employment under the 
programme is given to Below Poverty Lines (BPL) families. 
From 1.12.1997, Swarna Jayanti Sahari Rozgar Yojana (SJSRY) is the 
main poverty alleviation programme in the urban areas. The SJSRY, which 
has subsumed all the earlier three urban poverty alleviation programmes, 
viz., Nehru Rozgar Yojana (NRY), Urban Basic Services for the Poor 
(UBSP), Prime Minister's Integrated Urban Poverty Eradication Programme 
(PMIUPEP), seeks to provide gainful employment to unemployed or 
underemployed urban and educated up to IX standard for setting up self-
employment ventures or provision of wage employment. The 
implementation of SJSRY is relying on suitable community structures on the 
UBSP pattern and delivery of inputs u nder this programme is through the 
medium of Urban Local Bodies (ULBs) and such community structure.

4544. SHRI VEDPRAKASH P. GOYA L: Will the Minister of SMALL 
SCALE INDUSTRIES AND AGRO AND RURAL INDUSTRIES be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are awar e of the fact that the Small 
Scale, Agro and Rural Industries are facing severe threat from 
dumping of cheap foreign made goods and as per market estimates 40 per 
cent markets are flooded by these goods; 
(b) what steps arc being taken by Government to protect these industries; 
(c) the study, if any, conducted in this regard as why our domestic small 
and cottage industries, are not able to withstand the competition; 
(d) if so, what arc the findings thereof; and 
(e) the steps proposed by Government in this regard? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF SMALL SCALE 
INDUSTRIES AND AGRO AND RURAL INDUSTRIES (SHRIMATI 
VASUNDHARA RAJE): (a) and (b) Government have received information 
concerning unfair trade practices leading to import of cheap consumer goods 
causing injury to the domestic industry including small scale, agro and rural 
industries. The threat of injury to domestic products is being addressed 
through anti-dumping action, raising customs duty upto the bound levels and 
safeguard measures under the relevant WTO agreements. 
The Designated Authority appointed by the Government of India for 
conducting Anti-Dumping investigations in India has till date recommended 
imposition of anti dumping duties in 64 cases, preliminary duty in 19 cases 
and 6 cases are under investigation. The Government have also issued 
notification requiring compliance of all the conditions of the Standards of 
Weights and Measures (Packaged Commod ities) Order, 1977 on imports as 
applicable to domestic producers. Exporters to India of 131 products shall be 
required to register themselves with Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS) and 
their 
193 

RAJYA SABHA {26 April, 2001] 
products must comply with mandatory Indian quality standards. An intcr-ministcrial 
group under the Chairmanship of Commerce Secretary has been constituted to 
assess the impact of removal of quantitative restrictions and suggest suitable 
corrective measures. 
(c) to (c) Government is constantly  monitoring the impact of the WTO 
Agreements on the economy including the small scale, agro and rural industries 
in the country. The removal of Quantitative Restrictions (QRs) have exposed the 
Small Scale Industries (SSIs) to greater competition. Hence, Government 
have put in place several measures to help our industries become globally 
competitive. These include special focus on areas such as technology 
upgradation, infrastructure assist ance through cluster approach, timely 
availability of credit, adoption of ^modern management practices, use of 
electronic infrastructure arid other IT applications to face the emerging challenges 
of trade liberalization. A comprehensive policy package for the development 
of SSIs has been announced on 30th August, 2000. The policy package will 
enhance the competitiveness of SSIs through easier access to credit, availability of 
collateral free composite loan upto Rs. 25 lakhs capital subsidy for 
technology upgradation and improved infrastructure.

(c) The major accomplishment of Space Research in India is the self-reliant 
development of world class satellites and satellite launch vehicles and utilising 
the space systems in several areas relevant to national development in a cost 
effective manner. The multipurpose INSAT Satellite System which is one of the 
largest domestic satellite systems in the world is the main stay for the Television 
broadcasting services through connectivity to more than 1100 Television 
Transmitters, networking of radio stations, provision of cyclone warnings, 
gathering meteorological data, assisting weather forecasting and providing search 
and rescue support. These satellites are also extensively used for transmission of 
developmental programmes in rural areas and for educational training. The 
Indian Remote Sensing Satellite (IRS) system is among the best in the world for 
generating information useful for management of natural resources including 
location of zones of availability of ground water and monitoring of agricultural 
crops. The data from IRS satellites are used worldwide on a commercial basis. 
India's Polar Satellite Launch Vehicle (PSLV) is well proven through four 
successive successful flights and it provides self-reliant launch capability to 
orbit Remote Sensing Satellites of 1.2 ton class in polar sun synchronous orbits. 
The Geosynchronous Satellite Launch Vehicle (GSLV) has been successfully 
flight tested on 18th April, 2001, making India the sixth nation in the

world-wide that Indian Space Programme's Contributions to several areas of national

STATEMENT BY MINISTER 
Raids on Customs Officials 
THE MINISTER OF FINANCE (SHRI YASHWANT SINHA): 
Sir.Raids on premises of officers in connection with smuggling by 
Uzbek Nationals through IGI Airport, New Delhi. 
On 28 th August, 2000, an Uzbek woman was intercepted at 
IGI Airport, Delhi, while attempting to clear Chinese Silk without 
declaring them to the Customs Authorities. This lady had made 54 
trips to India during the period July 1999 to August 2000. The goods 
were seized under the Customs Act and the passenger was arrested 
and remanded to custody by the Additional Chief Metropolitan 
Magistrate. Her bail application was rejected by the ACMM on 14 th 
September, 2000, against which she filed an appeal before the 
Additional Sessions Judge. The Additional Sessions Judge, while 
allowing the appeal and granting bail, observed that there was a link 
with the Customs officials and that the CBI should investigate the role 
of customs officials.    The Commissioner of Customs preferred an 
appeal 
226 

[26 April, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
against the orders of the Additional Sessions Judge to the Delhi High 
Court, challenging grant of bail. In the meanwhile, she was detained 
under COFEPOSA Act and the matter was investigated in detail by 
the Director General of Revenue Intelligence and the Director General 
(Vigilance), CBEC. On the basis of the findings, 33 officers were 
suspended during February 2001, which included six Group 'A' 
officers. It was also decided to refer the matter to the CBI. The 
Department informed the High Court of this decision, when the matter 
came up for hearing in February, 2001 and referred the matter to CBI 
for investigation on 16 th February, 2001. The CBI have registered a 
case against 48 officers and four private persons on 30 m March, 2001, 
and conducted searches on the premises of these officers on 31" 
March, 2001. During raids, some cash, investments and property 
documents were recovered. None of the officers have been arrested 
by the CBI so far.  The matter Is still under investigation by the CBI, 
Raids on premises of former Chairman, Central Board of Excise 
and Customs. 
The Central Bureau of Investigation registered a case against 
Shri B.P. Verma, the former Chairm an of Central Board of Excise and 
Customs on 30* March, 2001 on the ba sis of source information on 
the allegation that, during the period from November, 2000 to March, 
2001, Shri B.P. Verma abused his official position and showed favour 
to M/s A.K. Enterprises, Chennai, in the matter of export of rags, 
declared as garments by the above mentioned firm, that he influenced 
his subordinate officers to enable the firm to draw false duty 
drawbacks, and that for this purpose, he obtained 
gratifications/considerations through his son. Consequent on the 
registration of the case, searches were conducted at the official as 
well as residential premises of Shri Verma on 31" March 2001. The 
CBI has reported that during the course of searches, several 
incriminating documents were seized . Scrutiny of these documents 
has revealed that Shri Verma is In possession of assets in his own 
name, in the name of his family members, as well as benami, which 
are prima facie disproportionate to his known sources of income. 
Accordingly, another case for posse ssing assets disproportionate to 
his known sources of income was also registered against him on 4 th 
April, 2001. Shri Verma was arrested by the CBi on 1" April, 2001, and 
remanded to custody. He was placed under suspension with effect 
from the date of his arrest.

SINGH): Mr. Chairman, Sir, what the hon. Finance Minister has told

responsible for collecting nearly sixty per cent of the total revenues of the 
Central Government. That the highest-ranking official of the Central 
Board of Customs and Excise should be charged with corruption is a 
very sad day for the Revenue administration. It is further saddening that it is

and Excise Department, some middlemen and even some people, whose

SHRI B.P. SINGHAL : Madam, the hon. Leader of the 
Opposition said ' it was a sad day when this bomb exploded in this 
country." What has been happening in  the country since the last 50 
years has to be cleaned up. Mr. Ramachandraiah rightly said that one 
sleaze after another would be exposed. Well, I am sure, as this 
Government is determined to clean up things, more sleazes will be 
exposed day after day and we need not be surprised. It is to the credit 
of this Government that it has taken the sternest action against the top 
man. I would like to congratulate the Minister of Finance for having the 
courage to have done this. And not only this; it was followed by 
widespread raids on the premises of other concerned officers, 
resulting in suspension of 30 other officers. Madam, it came about 
because accountability has suddenly di sappeared from this country. 
We talk of corruption. Madam, two cases, one after the other, were 
reported in the Press where Members of Parliament had given tickets 
to three or four women to undertake journey, with the help of other 
Members of Parliament, and they were caught by the TTE. It was a 
scandal of the worst kind. I brought this fact to the notice of the 
Chairman of the Ethics Committee and said " it has brought disgrace 
to the MPs,   whether they are of Lok Sabha or of Rajya Sabha."   I am 
sorry 
245 

RAJYA SABHA  [26 April. 2001] 
to say that he said "this is not a matter which comes under the 
jurisdiction of the Ethics Committee" and the matter ended there. If we 
are not willing to act swiftly against the acts of anybody, which gives 
an indication of immoral conduct, no matter, whosoever he may be, I 
am afraid, things will never improve. 
I do not suppose any other Government would have had the 
courage to disgrace the Chief of the Central Board of Customs and 
Excise, the manner in which he has been disgraced. His disgrace has 
been considered as the disgrace of the whole Department. Madam, I 
had been in the Police Service for 35 years. If you want to disgrace the 
Department, if you want to disgrace the police man, you support the 
wrong and they will get de moralised. I know it from my experience in 
Police Service. If it is made clear to every officer that no support will be 
granted to a wrong conduct, things will improve automatically. The 
corruption in the Customs Department has been pretty well known for 
years and years. I will give y ou one example. There was some 
clearance that was to be done in respect of a friend of mine. When he 
went for the clearance, he was told that whoever is shown as "Paid-up" 
on the official invoice - where they note down the items that have come 
to the warehouse, they tick-off the names of those persons from whom 
money has been received - they can get a smooth passage. Madam, 
such is the brazenness with which all this is going on. It has been 
going on not only for the last four-five years; it has been going on since 
a long time past. Madam, when I was in the police service, somebody 
asked me, "Why is the Police consi dered as a symbol of corruption." I 
said, "The answer is very simple." In the case of Police, Madam, if a 
police man takes money, immediately the third party is affected; and 
even a bribe of merely Rs. 10, that  is taken by a police man, is 
exposed. However, in cases where both the giver and the taker are 
happy, the exposure does not take pl ace. Actually, Madam, only when 
it reaches such proportions that things started stinking. Madam, 
generally there are three types of officers in every Department. One 
type of officers are those, who, wherever they stay, spread their 
fragrance and their fragrance goes even before they go to the next 
place of posting. The other type of officers are those who do not come 
out with any fragrance, but who do not stink either. And the third type 
of officers are those who stink. Now,  Madam, it is this type of officers, 
whose list is maintained by the CBI as well as by Vigilance Wing of the 
Department. It is a common list. Madam , my questions is : After this 
thing has come to light, would it not be proper to investigate thoroughly 
and scrutinise the assets of all those who are on the 
246 

[26 April, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
common list? At least, the assets of top five officials should be 
scrutinised so that they do not reach further heights in terms of getting 
promotions before they are clear ed by such scrutiny. The other 
question that I would like to ask is : What was the CVO of the 
Department doing? What was the Director of Revenue Intelligence 
doing? Why could not the CVO look into all these things? Is his work 
related only to sitting on the desk? Madam, such a serious thing has 
taken place and all those officers, who have contributed in ignoring the 
corrupt aspects of persons who have  been involved now at the junior 
levels and who have been giving them good chits, should be 
scrutinised. They should also be subjected to scrutiny. Any corrupt 
person in any Department, Madam, is pretty well known to all others, 
even if you cannot prove it. Such ca ses of corruption, where both the 
giver and the taker are happy, are very difficult to prove. But the stink 
is there. The bad reputation of a co rrupt official is there and on that 
basis, it can be easily distinguished as to who are those officers who 
are not worthy of being promoted beyond a certain level. The question 
that I would like to ask is : What action has been taken against the 
Senior Vigilance Officer who was su pposed to keep an eye on all that 
has been going on in the Customs Department? The next question is 
this. Madam, there seems to be a systemic failure. Sixty per cent of 
the corruption, whether it is in the Customs Department or in the Sales 
Tax Department or in the Police Department or anywhere else, takes 
place because of delays. I think it  is time that the people from the 
Revenue Intelligence should bring out a systemic change, calling for 
reporting of all delays. They can set out a reasonable period and any 
period of time spent beyond the stipulated time should be brought to 
the notice of Director of Revenue Intelligence. The officials should 
explain to the Director of Revenue Intelligence as to why a particular 
parcel which has arrived could not be cleared in a particular time-
frame. whichever is normal. 
Beyond that time, why this delay has taken place has to be 
explained. Each time those things would come on the computer, and it 
can be known. Delays should be curbed immediately. If I know that 
my goods will be cleared in five days or six days, whatever period has 
been fixed, I don't have to pay anyone. I will go there after five days 
and get my goods cleared. 
Madam, 60 per cent of the co rruption can be sealed off. I 
have done it in my Department. With top efficiency, corruption to the 
extent of 60-70 per cent can be pl ugged.  Then those people who are 
happy for what 
247 

RAJYA SABHA [26 April, 2001] 
one has done give you some award.   That is another matter.   But 
extortion definitely can be finished by this. 
Now, this lady made 54 trips.  Sure enough, there must be 
some systemic arrangement, by which if any person is making more 
than three or four or five or whatever number of trips during a 
particular period, during a year or so, eyebrows of the Customs 
officials should be raised. They should try to find out by checking his 
goods and finding out whether his visits are bona fide. Fifty-four in a 
year is too high, and it should have alerted those people, 
The trouble today, Madam, is about the amount of punishment 
that an officer has to undergo, I am saying "punishment" if he writes an 
adverse entry in any character roll,  it has to be communicated to the 
officer reported upon. The officer reported upon has to represent. A 
representation comes in 40 pages. So, if a person who has given an 
adverse entry and has been posted somewhere else, sees 40 pages, 
he has to address himself to each paragraph. That becomes a very big 
process. Today, officers are reluct ant to write frankly about what they 
feel about an officer on the basis of  his reputation. They just cannot 
write it because In the event of a representation, t hey will have to 
prove why they have arrived at that  decision. The other way also is 
there. If they were given the right to write the report confidentially, 
without that being communicated, corrupt persons may misuse it. They 
can ruin the careers of good people. So, some system has to be 
evolved in the writing of character rolls. The whole process has to be 
revised. Is the Finance Minister thinking of doing any such revision of 
how character rolls have to be written so that the true picture emerges 
and, at the same time, it does not provide material for wrongfully 
ruining a person's career? 
It has been said--and I want to support it-whoever have been 
instrumental in helping Mr. Verma to become a Board Member or 
Chairman, should be declared persona non grata, so far as this 
Government is concerned. They  have proven that they have the 
capability of backing the wrong horse, and their bona fides should be 
doubted for all times. I want to ask of the Finance Minister: has he got 
an idea about who were backing him up, and will he now mentally 
declare them as persona non grata, never to be heard again and their 
recommendations never to be considered? 
The unfortunate part is that complaints against corrupt people 
are not attended to. I have a case in point here, Madam. A person, a 
smalltime dealer, was coming from Singapore.   He was the last man 
to get his 
248 

[26 April, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
luggage. As he was going out, the Customs officials caught him and 
told him, "Oh, you have got this big box also? What is there in this big 
box?" He said, "This is not mine."  They said, "No.  This is yours."   He 
said, "This 
is not mine." They said, "It is your s," and they detained him. Then, the 
police was called and told, "This is his." The porters were there. They 
asked two porters, "Is it his?" They said, "No, this is not his." They said, 
"No, no. You do not know it." Madam, the recovery sheet was not 
written on that day because neither the porters nor the police personnel 
who were at the airport, would suppo rt them. The recovery sheet was 
written the next day. When this case came to me, I found that there 
were half-a-dozen clinching evidences to show that there was a big 
mischief. That particular box contained electronic goods worth about 
Rs.2 crores. 
And this man was hauled up. I spoke to the then Revenue 
Secretary. I told him that I am forwarding his complaint and requested him 
to have his case looked into. He said, "O.K. Send him to me." I told 
that man to come with all the facts, but he did not come. He came after 
twenty days. I asked him where he was all these days, i had made a 
complaint and I was in an awkward position. He told me that he was 
arrested and put in jail. Then I took his complaint and sent it to the 
Revenue Secretary. He promised that he would take action, but no 
action was taken. It was a brazenly wrong case. If the Finance Minister 
wants, I can still furnish all the details, but only on the condition that he 
will dig up that case, investigate and bring to book all those officers 
who perpetrated that mischief. It is because the corrupt are getting 
away that corruption thrives. 
With these words, I thank you very much for giving me the time.

some of the apprehensions which naturally and very legitimately have 
arisen in the minds of the hon. Members. Madam, I share the sadness 
expressed by the hon. Leader of the Opposition on these 
developments. I also believe that what has happened has opened the 
eyes of all of us, perhaps, more than it was in the past. 
And let me admit that as far as I am personally concerned, I 
have become far more alert, aware, of the need for vigilance after 
these recent events. At the same time, Madam Deputy Chairperson, I 
will entirely endorse the remarks which have been made by hon. 
Member, Shri S.S. Ahluwalia. This Department, this Board of Customs

Government of India collects in a year, and, therefore, it is a very, very

substantial powers under the law beca use they are at the frontiers of

of officers of this Department who have laid down their lives in the

Reserve Bank and the Credit Policy that we have announced on the 
^9m of March, have clearly said that, as far as the deposit schemes for 
senior citizens are concerned, banks  are permitted to formulate Fixed 
Deposit Schemes, specifically meant for senior citizens, offering them 
higher and fixed rates of interest, as compared to normal deposits of 
any size. The Reserve Bank has already mandated the banks to do 
this and, i hope, all the banks will come up with schemes so that senior 
citizens' problem is reduced. As far as the salaried class is concerned, 
and any loss that they might incur on their Provident Fund, etc., I have 
already announced yesterday in the other House that we are giving 
them more concessions by way of Standard Deduction in Income-tax 
and I am going to lose much more money than I am going to gain as a 
result of reduction in interest rates. So, as far as the interest rates are 
concerned, this is the position and I will plead very humbfy with this 
House that we should not have the kind of impressions that the hon. 
Member, Miss Mabel Rebello, had about small, small self-help groups 
which are being persuaded to deposit their earnings in the banks; if 
they earn more than Rs.2.500 by way of interest, the Income-tax is 
going to go after them. It is nothing. I have already explained that and 
in response to the point, a very valid point, that you made, Madam 
Deputy Chairperson, about micro finance as opposed to micro-credit. I 
entirely agree with you, and let me  tell you, that one of the major 
success stories of the last few y ears in this country -- and I am not 
merely referring to the last three years, during which I have been the 
Finance Minister; I am referring to the period before that also ~ has 
been the functioning of the self-help groups, largely of women, in the 
rural areas. I raised this point in the other House and I was informed by 
my colleague

from the Telegu Desam Party that 3,50,000 self-help groups of women

There were one or two points which were raised with 
reference to the Finance Bill. A gain on the abolition of the Banking 
Services Recruitment Boards, let me make it very clear. It does not 
mean that we are going to do away with reservation for Scheduled 
Castes and Scheduled Tribes. That is not the intention. The BSRBs 
will go because we had the Volu ntary Retirement Scheme for the 
public sector banks recently. Over a hundred thousand people 
voluntarily asked for retirement fr om bank service. Over a hundred 
thousand! 1,03,000 or thereabouts, to be precise! Now, in the light of 
this, we are trying to make a major shift in the banks' recruitment 
policy. We have said that banks must go in for highly skilled people. 
They must go in for people who understand the new technologies, the 
new financial products and, therefore,  it will be the recruitment of 
these specialised, qualified people in the banking industry in future. 
And, therefore, we have said that the bank boards will formulate -- and 
they have already formulated -- their own plans. I had mentioned it in 
response to a question the other day In this House. Their policies in 
the manpower planning have been formulated. The policies have been 
framed and whatever requirement is there, the bank boards will set up 
adequate mechanisms to make sure that recruitment is done in the 
best possible manner, keeping in mind the reservation principles of the 
Government. 
There was one last point, Madam Deputy Chairperson, or, one 
of the last points. I think I will take up two. One is th e question of this 
new dispensation that I have announced in the Finance Bill about 
Trusts, making their accounts public and getting them published in 
local newspapers. 
Now this has attracted a lot of attention and also criticism. I 
would hasten to add t hat i have amended the Fi nance Bill and raised 
the limit, of trusts which have to do this, from" Rs. 10 lakhs to Rs.1 
crore. Now, if a trust

a Task-Force which was set up by the Planning Commission, Madam 
Deputy Chairperson, for Voluntary Action Network India Group, and it was 
this Group which suggested that in order to bring greater transparency 
in the functioning of trusts, NGOs and others, this kind of a provision 
should be made. We have accepted their recommendation. We have 
mandated that they should publis h their account, not the detailed 
account, but the abridged account in the newspaper so that the people 
are aware of it. As far as the apprehension that mafia is going to get 
after them, I don't think there is anything which remains a secret in this

Madam Deputy Chairperson, one last point which has been 
raised by Jibonbabu is about the metallurgical coke. This is a very 
important issue, and I would like to take a minute of the House to explain 
this. When we are looking at the import duty structure, Madam Deputy 
Chairperson, I have reduced the totai number of import duty slabs to 
four. In Excise, i have reduced it to two. I had inherited a very large 
number of slabs. But over a period of time, I have brought them down 
to the minimum. I have given a clea r indication in my Budget Speech 
that we will move to the East Asian tariff levels in the next three years. 
I have asked the Department of Revenue to start working on this; 
whether we should have three rates of Customs Duty, or, whether we 
should have two rates of Customs Du ty. In the next Budget, we will be 
coming out with our plan of action on this. But why I am talking about 
metallurgical coke is that the steel industry was and continues to be in 
a serious problem. They are not able to compete even on the Indian 
soil because of various other reasons and one of them is the high cost 
of input; an£ metallurgical coke is a very important input for the steel 
industry. Shri Jibonbabu has been repeatedly saying that ,he has been in 
the trade union movement from the age of 16 or whatever. So, he will 
be in the trade union not only for metallurgical coke workers but also for 
the steel workers. So, metallurgical coke being an important thing, I 
looked at the figures, and I found that the total requirement of the 
country is something like 24 lakh tonnes of metallurgical coke. What is 
the total production? The totai production is three lakh tonnes. Now, we 
had a regime where in order to protect this three lakh tonnes, we had 
a very high rate of Customs Duty and at that high rate of Customs 
Duty, the steel industry was beco ming unviable and uncompetitive. 
That is why, in the amendment which I have
